Find the area of the triangle $△ABC.$

(Figure not drawn to scale)
questions.worked_solution:
The area of the triangle is defined as 

$$
A=\frac{b\cdot h}{2},
$$

 where $b$ is a base and $h$ is the corresponding height.

From the diagram, we see that the base is

$$
\begin{aligned}b & =AB \\  & =AH+HB \\  & =11+5 \\  & =16\end{aligned}
$$

and the corresponding height is

$$
h=CH=7.
$$

Therefore, the area is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{b\cdot h}{2} \\  & =\frac{16\cdot 7}{2} \\  & =\frac{112}{2} \\  & =56.\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13945897/assets/f8f748278d73c52d292e1b0545798507768cced623291a88df9175a4188ee976.png)

Consider the triangles $△ABC$ and $△CDE$ shown above. If the area of $△CDE$ is $18{\text{ cm}}^{2}$, find the area of $△ABC.$

(Figure not drawn to scale)
questions.worked_solution:
Let's consider $△CDE.$ We can see that $\overset{―}{CD}$ is the height corresponding to the base $\overset{―}{DE}$ and that $DE=6\text{ cm}.$ 

Since the area of $△CDE$ is $18{\text{ cm}}^{2},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{b\cdot h}{2} \\ 18 & =\frac{6\cdot CD}{2} \\ 3CD & =18 \\ CD & =6\text{ cm}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that $\overset{―}{CD}$ is also the height of $△ABC$ corresponding to the base $\overset{―}{AB}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13945897/assets/87c774cbdce6c4858605e2b8c6186abc6dde73b2b636966b4049ded4f82af684.png)

Therefore, we find the area of $△ABC$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{b\cdot h}{2} \\  & =\frac{AB\cdot CD}{2} \\  & =\frac{4\cdot 6}{2} \\  & =12{\text{ cm}}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{b\cdot h}{2} \\ 42 & =\frac{7\cdot CD}{2} \\ 7CD & =84 \\ CD & =12\text{ cm}.\end{aligned}

Now, notice that $\overset{―}{CD}$ is also the height of $△ABC$ corresponding to the base $\overset{―}{AB}.$

Find $AB$ given that the area of $△ABC$ is $140\,{m}^{2}$ and $CH=14\,m.$

(Figure not drawn to scale)
questions.worked_solution:
The formula for the area of the triangle is 

$$
A=\frac{b\cdot h}{2},
$$

 where $b$ is a base and $h$ the corresponding height.

From the diagram, we see that the base is $b=AB,$ and the corresponding height is 

$$
h=CH=14\,m.
$$

Therefore, using the formula for the area, we can solve for the base as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{b\cdot h}{2} \\ 140 & =\frac{b\cdot 14}{2} \\ 280 & =b\cdot 14 \\ b & =\frac{280}{14} \\ b & =20\,\text{m}\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, $AB=20\,\text{m}.$

Consider the triangles $△ABC$ and $△BCD$ shown above. If the area of $△BCD$ is $42{\text{ in}}^{2}$, find the area of $△ABC.$

(Figure not drawn to scale)
questions.worked_solution:
Let's consider $△BCD.$ We can see that $\overset{―}{BC}$ is the height corresponding to the base $\overset{―}{CD}$ and that $CD=12\text{ in}.$ 

Since the area of $△BCD$ is $42{\text{ in}}^{2},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{b\cdot h}{2} \\ 42 & =\frac{CD\cdot BC}{2} \\ 42 & =\frac{12\cdot BC}{2} \\ 84 & =12\cdot BC \\ BC & =\frac{84}{12} \\ BC & =7\text{ in}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that $\overset{―}{BC}$ is also the height of $△ABC$ corresponding to the base $\overset{―}{AB}.$ Therefore, we find the area of $△ABC$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{b\cdot h}{2} \\  & =\frac{AB\cdot BC}{2} \\  & =\frac{5\cdot 7}{2} \\  & =\frac{35}{2} \\  & =17.5{\text{ in}}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Find the area of the triangle $\triangle ABC.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13945897/assets/f892cd084f548769fa6b7352fece0e1aef3a66a4ab517ed5b5243d89041ac3a9.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The formula for the area of the triangle is

$$
\mathcal{A} = \dfrac{b \cdot h}{2},
$$

 

where $b$ is a base and $h$ is the corresponding height.

From the diagram, we see that the base is

$$
\begin{aligned}b & =AB \\  & =AH+HB \\  & =6+3 \\  & =9\end{aligned}
$$

and the corresponding height is

$$
h={CH} = 4 .
$$

Therefore, the area is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{b\cdot h}{2} \\  & =\frac{9\cdot 4}{2} \\  & =\frac{36}{2} \\  & =18.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the triangles $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle CDE$ shown below. If the area of $\triangle CDE$ is $25 \textrm{ cm}^2,$ find the area of $\triangle ABC.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13945897/assets/bd9840fd674fe7bf7b4f428591dfc6e9fbbaec8387836ece34694d17eaabe65b.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let's consider $\triangle CDE.$ We can see that $\overline{CD}$ is the height corresponding to the base $\overline{DE}$ and that $DE=10\textrm{ cm}.$ 

Since the area of $\triangle CDE$ is $25\textrm{ cm}^2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{b\cdot h}{2} \\ 25 & =\frac{10\cdot CD}{2} \\ 25 & =5\cdot CD \\ CD & =5\text{ cm}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that $\overline{CD}$ is also the height of $\triangle ABC$ corresponding to the base $\overline{AB}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13945897/assets/ea7f44b91e87a42029c5f00aae97a2eebf2e472ff890d4b91f4973e1e383e5c7.png)

Therefore, we find the area of $\triangle ABC$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{b\cdot h}{2} \\  & =\frac{AB\cdot CD}{2} \\  & =\frac{6\cdot 5}{2} \\  & =15{\text{ cm}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
